title: Using ecological restoration to disentangle the mechanisms and longevity of soil functional legacies
content:
Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog.


Abstract

Soil microbial functions are products of current and historical conditions, with the latter referred to as functional legacies. Functional legacies arising from land-use change have received less attention, despite evidence showing that these land use legacies alter contemporary microbial carbon (C) and nitrogen (N) cycling. We review the current evidence for land-use legacies, highlighting the effects of different agricultural management practices on soil microbial functions. We then present the functional legacy framework, which can be used to help explain persistent changes to soil biogeochemistry following land restoration or cessation of a land-use practice. Under this framework, altered belowground processes result from material and information legacies. Material legacies occur when resources from prior land-uses persist and drive microbial functions, whereas information legacies are changes to the functional potential of microbial communities from shifts in microbial populations or composition. Both legacies interact to maintain an altered or unexpected soil ecosystem state until new feedbacks emerge. To test the strength and longevity of material and information legacies, we detail potential experimental approaches for use within ecological restoration experiments. Restoration introduces new plant inputs to the resident soil microbial community and establishes new plant–microbial interactions, allowing investigators to trace potential material and information legacies and understand the underlying mechanisms. Applying the functional legacy framework across restoration experiments will help clarify the mechanisms of land-use legacies and improve predictions of belowground ecosystem recovery following future land restoration or perturbations.
